r2-across-1.name: r2-across-1
r2-across-1.statement: The RL-Zero-Math weight change acts, to first order, as a logit shift that collapses next-token entropy only at the base's own high-entropy fork positions and leaves low-entropy positions alone, so the RL model carries a fork-local low temperature: global temperature barely moves RL because its forks are already near one-hot, whereas for the base, cooling to T 0.6 also sharpens the easy restatement step at diffuse forks and starts loops, and heating to T 1.0 removes loops but samples wrong branches at the forks; any partial delta (attention-only, MLP-only, a times the delta) collapses fork entropy partly and stays temperature-sensitive in proportion to the fork entropy it leaves.

r2-across-2.name: r2-across-2
r2-across-2.statement: The RL-Zero-Math delta is small (0.24 % of weight norm) and sign-coherent: its function lies in the joint sign pattern of many coordinates, whose Fisher curvature on the base's own math samples is hundreds to thousands of times that of a random direction of the same norm, not in its large entries. So the effect of any edit is its energy divided by that leverage. Random resampling (DARE), random-sign or random-direction edits of the same norm, and magnitude-ranked subsets add almost nothing beyond their unbiased share of the sign pattern. The model's activations on general text barely move. The dose curve stays near-linear past a = 1. DARE fails only when its noise energy (1-q)/q exceeds the leverage, which puts the cliff at q of about 0.01-0.05 %. A large, low-coherence SFT delta (bytegraft, Think-SFT) fails all of these tests.

r3-revise-2.name: r3-revise-2
r3-revise-2.statement: A loop is an absorbing hazard for the cued base. The sampler opens it only at impasse positions, and how far along a solution impasses appear depends on the sampler: under T 0.6, impasses come early enough to trap medium-length solutions the base would otherwise finish, while at T >= 1.0 (with or without tail truncation) only a fixed, problem-specific set of long solutions reaches one, and those problems are mostly lost anyway. So a sampler moves accuracy only through loops it creates on finishable problems: accuracy is flat across T >= 1 samplers while cap hits vary, cap hits at T >= 1 are nested inside the T 0.6 cap-hit set, and many T 0.6 cap-hit problems are solved at T 1.0.

r4-m06.name: r4-m06
r4-m06.statement: RL added a roughly constant bias toward hold-on tokens and away from wrap-up tokens at every position, without a new error detector, so its extra re-checks land on right and wrong intermediate answers at the same added rate (on top of the base's own mild sensitivity to correctness), and accuracy rises only because re-checking a right answer rarely changes it while re-checking a wrong one sometimes does.

r4-m07.name: r4-m07
r4-m07.statement: The cued base's wrong answers are of two kinds, problem-specific attractors (one wrong value reached repeatedly by both base and RL, inherited from shared pretraining) and scattered slips; RL sharpens the base's own distribution, so it removes the scattered slips but keeps the attractors, which means RL's wrong answers mostly coincide with the base's repeated wrong answer and RL rarely fixes a problem on which the base has one.

r4-m08.name: r4-m08
r4-m08.statement: Part of the cued Olmo-3 base's accuracy comes from recalling solutions to problems that were in its pretraining text, which shows up as short, low-entropy right answers, while RL-Zero-Math learned procedures that also work on problems the base never saw; so at matched difficulty the RL-minus-cued-base gap is larger on problems published after the base's data cutoff (AIME 2025, HMMT Feb 2025) than on older problems, and smaller on problems the base can complete verbatim.

r4-m10.name: r4-m10
r4-m10.statement: In Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math, the early RL steps (100-400) concentrate the policy on the base's own high-probability paths, which raises accuracy on finished answers. The lower entropy also makes T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 sampling cross top-p's lock threshold more often, so looping cap hits rise above the base's. Only the slower pressure of 3.1's truncation-as-negative training later removes these loops, so cap hits at T 0.6 rise and then fall over training (base < step 100-400, step 2,800 far below the base).

r4-m11.name: r4-m11
r4-m11.statement: After stating an answer, the cued Olmo-3 base often fails to emit EOS and keeps writing like pretraining text (an invented follow-up problem, a variant, a reworking that changes the value). Grader v3 scores the last answer marker, so part of the cued base's MATH-500 deficit comes from answers whose first stated answer was right and were then overwritten by a later marker. RL boxes once and stops, so it does not carry this artifact.

r4-m12.name: r4-m12
r4-m12.statement: Part of the hard328 gap between RL and the cued base under grader v3 is grader false negatives: on problems whose gold answer is not an integer, the cued base often writes an equivalent but non-canonical final expression that the rule-based v3 rejects, while RL, shaped by its training verifier, writes the canonical simplified form that v3 accepts. So grader misses fall mostly on the base's finished answers to non-integer problems.

r4-m08-rival.name: r4-m08-rival
r4-m08-rival.statement: Exposure plays no part: the RL-minus-cued-base gap is set only by how long and hard a problem is, because the base fails to commit or terminate on long chains. The +6.9-point post-cutoff excess is single-sample noise on about 60 post problems, and short, low-entropy right answers are the generic confidence-length relation that any sampled model shows on easy problems.

r4-m10-rival.name: r4-m10-rival
r4-m10-rival.statement: By step 100, RL-Zero-Math has mainly taught the base to open in the RL model's own deliberation mode (the ' line!\n\nOkay' opening that the cue forces in the base), not a sharper, lower-entropy policy; at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 this long-deliberation mode loops exactly as the cued base does (119 cap hits vs 65 plain), so cap hits jump to roughly the cued-base level at step 100 and stay flat through step 400, until later commit-and-stop training (truncation negatives) removes them.

r5-account.name: r5-account
r5-account.statement: On MATH-500 at AI2's setting (T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample each), the 65 problems that Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math gets right and the cued Olmo 3 base gets wrong break down into four mechanisms and a small remainder. (1) Budget: about 0.25 are problems where the cued base ran to the 16,384-token cap without a loop. These are long problems on which the base keeps going and never commits, while RL, trained with truncated rollouts as negatives, finishes. (2) Answer statement: about 0.15 are problems where the base's failure was in stating the answer: a right value in a rejected or garbled final line, or a reached gold that it then overwrote. (3) Reliability: about 0.51 are problems the base solves in at least one of four other independent samples. The miss here is a sample-specific slip or misread on a problem the base can do, and RL removes it by concentrating on paths the base already samples. This is the largest part and the one still open. (4) Capability: about 0.07 are problems the base never solves in four further samples while RL solves at least two of four. Here RL uses a plan the base does not sample. (Unassigned) About 0.02 are problems where RL's single right answer was itself a lucky draw: RL is right in at most one of four other samples.

r6-account.name: r6-account
r6-account.statement: The problems that an RL-side model gets right and the cued Olmo 3 base gets wrong split into five mechanisms, applied in this order. (1) Loop: the base runs to the 16,384-token cap inside a self-reinforcing repeat (rule A). This is a sampler artifact of truncated, low-temperature decoding (T 0.6 / top-p 0.95). It is absent at T 1.0, and the base can usually do these problems at T 1.0. (2) Budget: the base hits the cap without a loop. These are long problems on which it never commits, while RL, trained with truncated rollouts as negatives, finishes. (3) Answer statement: the base finishes but writes no answer line, or writes the gold value in a box or 'Answer:' line and then ends on another value. (4) Reliability: the base solves the problem in at least one independent stored base sample, so the miss is a sample-specific slip that RL removes by concentrating on paths the base already samples. (5) Capability: no independent base sample solves it. On the known cell (MATH-500, T 1.0, cued base against Olmo-3.1 RL) the shares are 0 / 0.25 / 0.15 / 0.54 / 0.06. I predict how the shares move in three other cells. Against the half-dose weight blend theta0.5 at T 1.0, budget falls to about 0.17 and reliability rises to about 0.70, because theta0.5 keeps almost the base's cap rate but already has the sharpening. On hard328 against Code-RL at T 1.0, the shares are loop 0.02, budget 0.25, answer 0.08, reliability 0.34 and capability 0.31: capability grows on the harder set, where the base's independent evidence is weaker. On MATH-500 at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 against RL step 400 (grader v1), loop takes about 0.50, with budget 0.13, answer 0.17 (v1 misses on the base's 'Answer:' lines), reliability 0.15 and capability 0.05. The largest part still open at T 1.0 is reliability, and the base-only route to it is more independent votes, weighted toward high-precision finished answers.
